newsitem.title: DENMARK: Denmark says EU referendum not before March 1998.
newsitem.headline: Denmark says EU referendum not before March 1998.

text.p: Foreign Minister Niels Helveg Petersen said on Tuesday that Denmark would hold a referendum on last June's Amsterdam amendments to the European Union treaty some time after mid-March 1998.

"That gives us plenty of time for debate. We have only just begun the discussion and the referendum will be in seven months from now, at the earliest," he told reporters at the ministry's weekly briefing.
He added that the government would propose a firm date after parliament reconvenes from its summer recess, in October, and there would then be further debate.

A Supreme Court ruling on a challenge by a group of Danish citizens to the legality of Danish membership of the EU was also expected in March, the petitioners' lawyer said last month, but Petersen said he foresaw a verdict earlier.

"It is my evaluation today that the constitutional case which several people have put before the courts will be finished in good enough time to avoid conflict with the date for the referendum," he said.
The petitioners say that Denmark has ceded authority to supranational institutions, such as the European Court, to an extent that breaches its own national constitution.
Danes are traditionally cool toward the EU. They shocked their fellow members in 1992 by flatly rejecting the Maastricht Treaty on closer European cooperation in a referendum.
They only voted to ratify the treaty the following year on condition that Denmark opt out of economic and monetary union, a joint defence structure, cross-border policing and a common asylum policy.
An opinion poll last week showed that 32 percent of respondents would vote to accept the Amsterdam treaty, 31 percent would reject it and 36.5 were unsure.

EU leaders decided at Amsterdam to leave the Western European Union defence grouping independent of the union, to grant Britain and Ireland opt-outs from a plan to lift internal border checks, to make job creation a formal EU goal, and to increase cooperation in foreign policy and asylum policy.
The summit left key institutional reforms to be taken early next century.

Petersen and Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen have warned that a referendum "no" vote would undermine Denmark's efforts to expand the EU eastward, that uncertainty as to Demark's future status in the Union could lessen its influence and that the Amsterdam amendments would fail to go into force.

Politicians in both the opposition and ruling centre-left coalition have labelled such comments as scaremongering and say that attempting to scare voters into a "yes" vote could panic them instead into a rejection of the accord.
